document.abstract: We present a layout-first pipeline that converts scientific PDFs into structured, page-grounded documents. Instead of relying on a single  text-extraction  pass,  the  pipeline  segments  each  page  into  blocks,  classifies  them,  orders  them  by  a  column-aware reading-order  model,  and  reconstructs  tables  and  equations  as  structured  objects.  On  a  benchmark  of  120  papers,  the  method reaches a word-level F1 of 0.982 and a table cell accuracy of 0.941, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.4 points.

evidence_text: We evaluate on DocBench-120, a collection of 120 papers from  six  publishers,  of  which  18  are  scanned  images without  a  text  layer.  Each  paper  was  annotated  by  two students  with  block  boundaries,  reading  order  and  table structure;  disagreements  were  resolved  by  a  third annotator. Table 2 reports the per-document-type breakdown.  The  runtime  of  the  full  pipeline  is  1.8  s  per page  on  a  single  CPU  core,  compared  with  4.1  s  for  the strongest baseline, a 2.3× speed-up.

Naive extraction that sorts glyphs by their vertical position interleaves  the  two  columns  of  a  double-column  page, producing  sentences  that  read  "the  model  was  trained  on 12,431  pairs  of  images  and  achieves  state-of-the-art results"  out  of  two  unrelated  paragraphs.  Downstream translation and question answering then inherit these errors silently. This paper argues that the ordering problem must be solved at the level of layout blocks rather than individual characters,  and  that  every  extracted  span  should  carry  a pointer back to the page region it came from.
